title: The Wife's Device and the Signet Ring

keywords: the wife's device to cheat her husband
full_text:
In Damascus lived an affluent linen-merchant who was constantly plagued by groundless suspicions, imagining that his loyal and prudent wife was secretly careless with his household goods.

One morning, having misplaced his gold signet ring, the merchant accused his wife of having dropped it in the street or given it away to a peddler, threatening to divorce her if it was not recovered by sunset.

The wife, knowing that her husband had simply left the ring in his ledger book in his bazaar stall, resolved to cure his suspicious temper with a harmless comedy.

She baked a large, round meat pie stuffed with minced lamb, pistachios, and spices, leaving a hollow crust at the top. Walking to the bazaar at noon, she presented the pie to her husband for his lunch, whispering: 'O husband, eat of this pie, and ask the heavens to restore your lost treasure.'

The merchant broke open the pie and found inside a carved wooden turnip fashioned into the likeness of a ring, with a small folded parchment:
'The ring you seek rests inside the seventh page of your ledger book;
He who suspects his wife of theft should look inside his own pocket!'

The merchant turned red with embarrassment. He opened his ledger, turned to the seventh page, and there lay his gleaming gold signet ring, where he had placed it himself to mark an account!

Ashamed of his hasty accusations, the merchant brought home gifts of silk and sweetmeats, begged his wife’s forgiveness, and never again allowed suspicion to disturb the domestic peace of their home.
moral: Trust in marriage is a sacred bond; testing it with suspicion invites harmless but sharp wit.
